body: General Electric traded ~$30-32 in mid-2016 and fell to ~$6.7 by Dec 2018 (-58% in 2018 alone, worst year in >50 years; pre-2021 1:8 reverse split). Sequence: Nov 2017 dividend halved; Jan 2018 a $6.2 bn after-tax charge on run-off long-term-care insurance plus ~$15 bn of statutory reserve contributions over 7 years; Oct 2018 a $22 bn goodwill impairment in GE Power (largely Alstom, bought 2015) and dividend cut to $0.01; SEC/DOJ probes; 2019 Markopolos report alleged further LTC under-reserving (GE disputed). Recovery came only after Larry Culp's deleveraging and the break-up into GE Aerospace, GE Vernova and GE HealthCare (2023-24). Visible flags: (1) industrial CFO flattered by selling receivables to GE Capital ('factoring') and 'deferred monetisation' of service contracts (contract assets growing faster than revenue); (2) dividend exceeding free cash flow; (3) a long-tail insurance liability inside an industrial company; (4) Alstom paid at the power cycle peak -> goodwill; (5) consistent 'beat by a penny' earnings and heavy non-GAAP adjustments; (6) repeated CEO changes in 2017-18. Lesson: a low P/E on 'normal' earnings is a trap when earnings quality is low; check contract assets, receivable sales and dividend cover by FCF. Index weight and history are not safety.

data.early_signals: receivable factoring to boost CFO; contract assets; dividend > FCF; LTC insurance; Alstom goodwill
data.lesson: Low P/E on poor-quality earnings is a value trap

title: GE 2017-2018: blue-chip value trap

body: Lehman peaked ~$86 in Feb 2007 and filed for bankruptcy on 15 Sep 2008 ($639 bn assets, largest in US history). Leverage (assets/equity) was ~30x at end-2007; a large share of assets were illiquid commercial real estate (incl. the Archstone deal), private equity and Level 3 positions marked by models. The bankruptcy examiner (Valukas, 2010) found 'Repo 105' transactions moved ~$50 bn of assets off the balance sheet at quarter-ends in 2008 to show lower net leverage -- 'materially misleading'. Visible flags: (1) leverage ~30x with short-term repo funding; (2) Level 3 assets exceeding shareholders' equity; (3) slow write-downs versus peers -- David Einhorn (Greenlight) publicly argued in Apr-May 2008 that Lehman's marks and its CDO/CRE exposure were understated and that it raised capital while reporting profits; (4) widening CDS spreads and Bear Stearns' Mar 2008 failure as a template; (5) capital raises in Jun 2008 at discounts; (6) quarter-end balance sheet 'window dressing'. Lesson: for levered financials, equity is a thin sliver -- a 3-4% asset write-down wipes it; quarter-end vs average balance sheet gaps and Level 3/equity ratios are key tests. Altman Z and M-score don't apply; use leverage, funding tenor and mark-to-market tests.

data.early_signals: 30x leverage; Level 3 > equity; Repo 105 window dressing; Einhorn critique; CDS widening
